1.pericope_label: And the LORD spake unto Moses, saying, Speak unto the children of Israel, and take of every one of them a rod according to the house of their fathers, of all their princes according to the house of their fathers twelve rods: write thou every man's name upon his rod. And thou shalt write Aaron's name upon the rod of Levi: for one rod shall be for the head of the house of their fathers. And thou shalt lay them up in the tabernacle of the congregation before the testimony, where I will meet with you. And it shall come to pass, that the man's rod, whom I shall choose, shall blossom: and I will make to cease from me the murmurings of the children of Israel, whereby they murmur against you. And Moses spake unto the children of Israel, and every one of their princes gave him a rod apiece, for each prince one, according to their fathers' houses, even twelve rods: and the rod of Aaron was among their rods. And Moses laid up the rods before the LORD in the tabernacle of witness.

schools.summary: Calvin explains why the priesthood had to be settled rather than shared: sacrifices belonged to the whole people but were to be offered by one man in one place, lest altars everywhere corrupt the worship by variety, and in order to point the people to the Mediator through whom alone an offering is acceptable. On the count of the rods he denies flatly that a thirteenth was added for Levi, and gives the reason the others miss — Joseph was divided in two only where land was at stake, and here nothing turns on territory. He reads Aaron’s rod being in the midst of them as ordinary Hebrew for mingled among them, stated expressly to leave no ground for cavilling. Gill dates the episode to just after the plague and observes that writing the tribal name would have settled nothing, since the quarrel was inside the tribe of Levi.

Henry notes that the word for a rod is also the word for a tribe, and reasons from the princes’ willingness to compete: the priesthood was plainly a preferment worth striving for, and serving God is an honour to the greatest of men, though he suspects the contenders wanted the profit and power rather than the sacredness of the office. What strikes him most is the persistence — that after all that had been done to settle the matter men were still ready to reopen it, striving with God for the dominion.

Wesley identifies the rod as the staff a prince carried as the badge of his authority, and explains why each prince’s own name was required: as firstborn and chief they had the strongest claim if the priesthood were open to their tribes, and each represented his whole tribe, so the trial decided the question completely. He points out that one might have expected two rods for Levi, one for Aaron and one for his rivals within the tribe, and that the single name settled tribe and family together; and he infers from the whole arrangement that men of other tribes, not only Korah and the Levites, had been pressing the claim.

Ellicott lays out both accounts of the twelve rods and prefers the one that makes Ephraim and Manasseh a single tribe of Joseph, on the wording and on the parallel where Levi is counted among the twelve; he explains that Aaron, descended from Levi’s second son, was the appointed rather than the natural head of his house, and notes that writing a name on a rod matched an Egyptian custom and a later prophetic sign. Keil reaches the same conclusion about Joseph independently, and renders the promise attached to the blossoming rod by the causative force of its verb, to make sink or bring to rest, so that what the sign accomplishes is the quieting of the murmuring.

debates: Whether there were twelve rods including Levi or thirteen including Aaron’s.
Whether Ephraim and Manasseh counted as one tribe here or two.
Why Aaron’s name was written rather than Levi’s.
Who was actually contending for the priesthood.
Why the priesthood had to be confined to one family at all.
outliers: Calvin names and rejects the reading that adds a thirteenth rod, and grounds his own on the absence of any territorial question.
Wesley asks why Levi did not receive two rods, one for Aaron and one for his competitors, and answers from the sufficiency of the name.
Ellicott compares the inscribing of names on rods to an Egyptian practice and to a prophetic sign.
Henry suspects the contenders were after the profit and power of the office rather than its sacredness.
Keil gives the verb of the promise its causative force, so that the sign is meant to quiet the people rather than merely to identify a man.
themes: Twelve rods, one for each prince
Aaron’s name upon the rod of Levi
The man’s rod whom I shall choose shall blossom

8.pericope_label: And it came to pass, that on the morrow Moses went into the tabernacle of witness; and, behold, the rod of Aaron for the house of Levi was budded, and brought forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and yielded almonds. And Moses brought out all the rods from before the LORD unto all the children of Israel: and they looked, and took every man his rod. And the LORD said unto Moses, Bring Aaron's rod again before the testimony, to be kept for a token against the rebels; and thou shalt quite take away their murmurings from me, that they die not. And Moses did so: as the LORD commanded him, so did he.

schools.summary: Calvin asks why the rod was to be preserved and answers from human forgetfulness: men are slow to consider God’s works and bury the memory of them as if on purpose, so the reason given for laying up the sign is their own perverseness, which he takes as a reproach. He then finds mercy in the same command, since a people so inclined to rebel would have provoked God again, and the token forestalls them so that they do not die; humbling us, God both punishes and consults our good. Gill holds that the place Moses entered was open to him at any time.

Henry rests the proof on the three stages appearing at once. Buds, blossoms and ripe fruit on one dry staff could not be counterfeited by substituting a living bough overnight, because no natural branch carries all three together; and the sign marks Aaron as under a blessing of heaven that yields increase where nobody has planted or watered.

Clarke identifies the wood as the common almond, describes the tree’s habit and early flowering, and derives its Hebrew name from a root meaning to awake. He reads the three stages devotionally, as the buds of good desire, the blossoms of resolution and profession, and the ripe fruit of faith and love and obedience, all deriving from the priesthood of Christ. Wesley raises the difficulty of Moses entering the most holy place, which belonged to the high priest alone and to him once a year, and answers it from the express command under which he went.

Ellicott corrects the rendering to say the rod brought almonds to maturity, and derives the tree’s name from the verb to keep watch rather than to awake, explaining it by its blossoming while other vegetation sleeps. He reads the sign typologically, of Christ as the rod from the stem of Jesse and of the Spirit’s working in the ministry. On the rod’s later history he is careful: the text never says it was placed inside the ark, the ark held only the tables when it entered Solomon’s temple, and that fact does not contradict the epistle’s account of an earlier period; he adds the tradition that the rod was hidden with the ark, still bearing buds.

debates: Whether the almond’s name derives from waking or from watching.
Whether Moses might lawfully enter the most holy place, and on what warrant.
Whether the rod was placed inside the ark or before it.
How the ark holding only the tables in Solomon’s day squares with the epistle’s account.
Why the rod had to be preserved after the question was settled.
outliers: Henry rests the proof against fraud on buds, blossoms and fruit appearing simultaneously, which no natural branch does.
Clarke and Ellicott derive the same Hebrew name from cognate roots and give it two different senses.
Gill and Wesley differ over who might enter the most holy place and on what terms.
Ellicott argues that a statement about the ark’s contents at one date settles nothing about an earlier one.
Ellicott preserves a tradition that the rod was hidden with the ark and still bore buds when it was.
Calvin reads the preservation of the token as simultaneously a reproach and an act of fatherly care.
themes: The rod of Aaron was budded
That thou mayest take away their murmurings

12.pericope_label: And the children of Israel spake unto Moses, saying, Behold, we die, we perish, we all perish. Whosoever cometh any thing near unto the tabernacle of the LORD shall die: shall we be consumed with dying?

schools.summary: Calvin refuses to take alarm for piety. It is better than stupid contempt, but the mean between torpor and panic is missing here: a believer’s fear humbles him and still sends him toward God, while this fear wishes God further off. Having no sense of his goodness, Israel felt the chastisement as a gibbet rather than a medicine, though he grants that servile fear may sometimes prepare the way for repentance. Gill draws the same contrast historically, between men who lately claimed the priesthood and now dare not approach the tabernacle, and reports that the versions render the closing clause as a statement rather than a question, which he prefers as fitting the context better.

Clarke glosses the verb as describing suffocation rather than death simply, and uses the cry to expose a pendulum: the people who had claimed that everyone was holy enough to minister now believe nobody may approach at all, and are wrong both times, because God had drawn a line that should have settled it. Wesley reads the outburst as consternation with three sources — the memory of repeated judgments, the threat hanging over any further murmuring, and their own sense of guilt and of a weakness likely to relapse — and takes the closing clause as a genuine question about whether strict justice will consume them all.

debates: Whether the closing clause is a question or an affirmation.
Whether the people’s fear was a step toward repentance or a flight from God.
What the verb behind their cry actually describes.
Whether their new caution was any more correct than their former presumption.
outliers: Clarke treats the people’s two positions as a single error running to opposite extremes.
Calvin distinguishes a fear that drives a man toward God from one that wishes God away, and puts Israel in the second class.
Gill prefers the affirmative rendering of the last clause on the ground that men do not question what they have just asserted.
Wesley traces the panic to the memory of past judgments and the fear of relapsing into the same fault.
themes: Shall we be consumed with dying
